what_its_for: Trastuzumab-anns is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of breast cancer and stomach cancer that have too much of a protein called HER2. It works by attaching to HER2 proteins on cancer cells and helping your immune system find and destroy them. It may be used alone or together with other cancer medicines.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or IV line. A healthcare provider, such as a nurse or doctor, will give you this medicine in a clinic or hospital setting. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion usually takes 30 to 90 minutes. Your first infusion may take longer so your care team can watch for any reactions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body weight and the type of cancer being treated. Most patients receive this medicine either once every week or once every 3 weeks. Your treatment schedule will be planned specifically for you by your cancer care team. Do not change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an infusion appointment, contact your doctor or cancer care team as soon as possible. They will help you figure out the best time to reschedule your treatment. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home, as it is prepared and given by healthcare professionals. The clinic or pharmacy will store it properly in a refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Keep it away from freezing and direct light.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as this medicine can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 7 months after stopping. Avoid getting live vaccines during treatment without asking your doctor first. Let your doctor know about all other medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as some may interact with this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following: trouble breathing, shortness of breath, or wheezing; chest pain or tightness; swelling of the ankles or feet; rapid weight gain; irregular heartbeat or pounding in your chest; severe chills, fever, or shaking during or after your infusion; severe nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea; unusual bruising or bleeding; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat; or feeling dizzy or faint. These may be signs of serious side effects including heart problems or infusion reactions.
when_it_works: It may take several weeks to months before you or your doctor can tell if this medicine is working. Your doctor will check your progress regularly using blood tests, imaging scans, or other tests. Do not stop treatment on your own even if you feel well, because this medicine needs time to do its job. Stay in close contact with your cancer care team throughout your treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy: This medicine can cause serious harm or death to an unborn baby. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant during treatment. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for 7 months after your last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 7 months after your last dose. Older adults: Older patients may be at a higher risk for heart-related side effects. Your doctor will monitor your heart closely. Heart conditions: Tell your doctor if you have any history of heart problems, as this medicine can weaken the heart. Your heart function will be tested before and regularly during treatment. Children: The safety and use of this medicine in children has not been fully established. Talk to your doctor if you have questions about use in a younger patient.
